name: sish
last_commit_or_release_date: Active — 345 commits on main, recent commits/releases visible, ongoing releases via goreleaser and Docker image publishing (checked 2026)
maturity_notes: Actively maintained, well-documented, production-oriented (used to run a managed public service tuns.sh, sponsored by pico.sh). No obvious red flags; healthy commit cadence, CI (golangci-lint), Docker images, binary releases.
popularity_signal: 4.7k GitHub stars, 335 forks, 54 watchers — clearly the most popular of the four tools surveyed, used in production by a public managed tunnel service.
infra_lift_on_sveltekit_node: sish is a standalone Go SSH server binary (main.go, cmd/, sshmuxer/, httpmuxer/ packages) — it is NOT embeddable inside a Node.js process. It must run as a separate long-lived service/binary (or Docker container) on our cloud infra, listening on an SSH port (e.g. 2222) plus HTTP(S)/WS(S) ports for tunnel traffic, with its own TLS cert management, key-based auth files, and routing config. Our SvelteKit backend would sit behind/alongside it, or sish's HTTP muxer would need to front our app's routes — effectively adding a whole new infra component (process supervision, port allocation, key management, DNS wildcard) that must be deployed and operated independently from the Node app.
client_side_simplicity: Excellent — client-side needs literally nothing beyond a standard OpenSSH client already present on virtually every OS (`ssh -R 80:localhost:8080 tuns.sh`). No admin/root required, no special binary to install, no network interface management. This is the best-in-class client experience of all 4 options.
loc_estimate_and_admin_burden: Near-zero client integration LOC (just shell out to ssh or use an SSH library like Go's golang.org/x/crypto/ssh or Node's ssh2 to establish -R forwarding programmatically, ~50-150 LOC for a managed client wrapper). Server-side: deploying/operating sish itself is the real burden — new binary/container, systemd unit or k8s deployment, SSH host key management, authorized_keys or dynamic key issuance for each user, TLS cert automation, monitoring a second service. Ongoing ops burden is moderate-to-high: it's essentially standing up and maintaining a bespoke SSH-tunnel PaaS.
viability_notes: Best-in-class client simplicity (no custom client at all, just SSH) makes this attractive for zero-admin-burden goals, but it fails the 'minimal infra' priority hard — it requires running and operating an entirely separate SSH server process/binary with its own auth and TLS lifecycle, which is more infra than our current custom WS design. Worth considering only if we're willing to trade infra complexity for client simplicity; not a drop-in replacement for embedding in the existing Node process.

name: koding/tunnel
last_commit_or_release_date: Last commit June 1, 2017 — no commits, releases, or activity in ~8+ years as of this research (2026 check)
maturity_notes: Effectively abandoned/unmaintained. README itself states 'under active development, please vendor it if you want to use it' — a warning sign this was never considered stable, and now it has been stagnant for nearly a decade. No recent commits, no CI activity, low watcher count (18). Major red flag for adopting this as a foundational dependency in new infrastructure.
popularity_signal: 331 stars, 69 forks — modest niche popularity from the ~2016 Koding platform era; not a widely adopted current standard.
infra_lift_on_sveltekit_node: This IS a Go library (not Node), so despite being conceptually a 'library not a binary,' it is NOT embeddable inside our Node.js/SvelteKit process at all — Go and Node are different runtimes with no in-process interop. To use koding/tunnel we would still need to write and run a separate Go binary/process on our cloud infra that imports tunnel.NewServer() and satisfies http.Handler, then either reverse-proxy Node traffic into it or run it as a sidecar in front of/behind the SvelteKit app. So in practice it has the same 'separate process required' infra lift as the other Go options — the 'library' framing only helps if your cloud backend is also Go, which ours is not.
client_side_simplicity: Client is also a Go binary/library (tunnel.NewClient) requiring a compiled Go client executable on the end-user's machine, or us cross-compiling and shipping a small Go binary for their OS/arch. No admin/root or interface management needed (pure userspace TCP dial), but it does require distributing and running a compiled binary rather than reusing something already installed — more client packaging burden than SSH-based sish.
loc_estimate_and_admin_burden: Server integration: a Go microservice (~100-300 LOC to configure ServerConfig, AddHost, wire yamux) that must be built, deployed, and kept running as a separate process from the Node app — plus ongoing burden of a stale/unmaintained dependency (potential security/CVE exposure with zero upstream fixes). Client: needs Go toolchain to build/cross-compile a client binary bundled with our Python wrapper, adding packaging complexity (multi-arch binaries) atop the existing Python distribution.
viability_notes: Despite superficial appeal as a 'library,' koding/tunnel is a Go library usable only from Go processes — it cannot be embedded in our Node/SvelteKit server, so it doesn't reduce infra lift as hoped, and it also requires a separately built/shipped Go client binary. Combined with ~8 years of zero maintenance and an explicit 'vendor it, use at your own risk' warning in the README, this is not a viable choice.

name: h2tunnel
last_commit_or_release_date: Actively maintained — commits as recent as Aug 28, 2026 (dependency bump) and Jun 14/17, 2026 (feature/doc work); regular npm releases via automated GitHub Actions publishing with provenance attestation.
maturity_notes: Small but genuinely active project with a real author blog post explaining the design (boronine.com, June 2025), CI on GitHub Actions, test suite with coverage reporting, and recent dependency/security maintenance (dependabot bumps merged same year). Codebase is deliberately tiny ("less than 500 LOC", h2tunnel.ts) and zero-dependency, which minimizes supply-chain risk. Not battle-tested at scale (only 142 stars, 2 watchers) but the code is auditable in an afternoon given its size.
popularity_signal: 142 stars, 4 forks — niche/early-stage project, much smaller community than sish or go-http-tunnel, but published on npm (h2tunnel) with real version history and active issue/PR engagement from the author.
infra_lift_on_sveltekit_node: YES — this is the standout finding: h2tunnel exports a `TunnelServer` class directly usable as a plain Node.js library, no separate binary needed. Integration would be: `npm install h2tunnel`, then in our existing Node/adapter-node server process: `import { TunnelServer } from "h2tunnel"; const server = new TunnelServer({ key, cert, tunnelListenIp: "::0", tunnelListenPort: 15900, proxyListenIp: "::0", proxyListenPort: <port> }); server.start(); await server.waitUntilListening();` — roughly 10-20 lines of glue code to instantiate, start, and wire lifecycle (start on app boot, stop on shutdown), plus generating/rotating the mTLS cert+key pair (a few more lines using Node's crypto or a setup script). It listens on its OWN TCP ports (tunnelListenPort for client connections, proxyListenPort for public HTTP traffic) inside the SAME Node process — no separate deployable artifact, though it does need extra listening ports open on the same host/container as SvelteKit, and a reverse proxy (e.g. Caddy) or manual HTTP routing to stitch its proxied traffic into the SvelteKit app if we want a single public origin.
client_side_simplicity: Also just an npm library — `import { TunnelClient } from "h2tunnel"` requires Node.js on the client machine (we already run Node for the wrapper? — actually our client is Python, so this would mean bundling a Node runtime for the local client, OR reimplementing the tiny HTTP/2+mTLS protocol in Python). No admin/root or interface management needed — it's a pure userspace outbound TLS connection. The catch for our stack specifically: it's Node-only out of the box, so a Python-based llama-server wrapper would need to either shell out to a bundled Node binary or reimplement the protocol.
loc_estimate_and_admin_burden: Server-side glue: ~20-50 LOC to embed TunnelServer in our existing Node/SvelteKit process, plus a cert-generation/rotation script (~30-50 LOC, one-time mTLS keypair per client or shared secret). Client-side: if reimplementing in Python (since our client is Python, not Node), meaningfully more work (~300-500 LOC to reimplement the documented HTTP/2 mTLS protocol using Python's h2/hyper libraries) OR bundling a Node sidecar binary (~50 LOC glue + packaging burden). Ongoing ops burden is low on the server side (it's in-process, scales/restarts with the app) but the project's small community means we'd be one of few consumers — some risk of needing to patch/fork it ourselves for edge cases.
viability_notes: This is the most infra-efficient option for the SERVER side — it truly embeds as a library in our existing Node/SvelteKit process with minimal glue code, directly satisfying the 'no separate binary' goal, and requires zero client admin permissions. The main friction is that our client is Python, not Node, so we'd either need to reimplement its small, well-documented mTLS+HTTP/2 protocol in Python or ship a Node sidecar — a real but bounded and worthwhile tradeoff given how much server-side infra it saves versus our custom APLC-1 build.

name: go-http-tunnel
last_commit_or_release_date: Last meaningful commit was a dependency bump on Apr 19, 2024 (golang.org/x/net); prior substantive feature work (websocket support) from Jul 2022; project has slowed significantly (long gaps between commits: 2020 → 2022 → 2023 → 2024) but is not formally archived.
maturity_notes: Popular and historically well-regarded, but maintenance has clearly slowed to occasional dependency-bump commits rather than active feature development; author (mmatczuk, a recognized Go engineer) still merges occasional PRs. AGPL-3.0 license is a notable red flag/consideration: it requires that any network-service use of the code be made available in source form (with a paid "enterprise license" alternative offered by the author) — this has real legal/business implications for embedding it in a commercial SaaS backend.
popularity_signal: 3.3k stars, 312 forks, 61 watchers — the second most popular tool in this survey after sish, reflecting real historical adoption, though momentum has cooled.
infra_lift_on_sveltekit_node: Pure Go library/binary (cmd/ contains tunneld server and tunnel client binaries) — no Node interop possible. Would require deploying a separate Go binary (tunneld) as its own process/container on our cloud infrastructure, exposing its own TLS-terminated port for client connections and proxying HTTP/2-multiplexed traffic to our SvelteKit app's port, essentially the same 'extra service to build, deploy, and operate' pattern as go-http-tunnel's stablemates (sish, koding/tunnel). Additionally, the AGPL-3.0 license would legally obligate us to release our modifications/integration source (or purchase mmatczuk's enterprise license) since we'd be offering it as part of a network service — a meaningful business decision, not just an engineering one.
client_side_simplicity: Requires running the project's own compiled Go `tunnel` client binary on the end-user's machine (cross-compiled per OS/arch), authenticated via TLS client certificates. No root/admin or interface management needed — it's a normal userspace process — but like koding/tunnel, it means shipping/bundling an extra platform-specific binary alongside our Python client rather than reusing an existing installed tool.
loc_estimate_and_admin_burden: Server: deploying tunneld as a managed service (~100-200 LOC of Go config/wiring on top of the existing binary, or use as-is via CLI flags) plus systemd/container lifecycle management, TLS cert issuance per client, and DNS/host-mapping config. Client: bundling a compiled Go binary with the Python wrapper (packaging LOC modest, ~50-100 LOC of subprocess glue in Python, but multi-arch binary distribution adds release-engineering overhead). Ongoing burden: moderate — one more service to patch/monitor, plus AGPL compliance review before shipping.
viability_notes: Technically solid HTTP/2-based multiplexing tunnel with decent adoption, but it fails the 'no separate infra' goal just as much as sish (a whole extra Go service to run and operate), it needs a bundled Go client binary rather than an already-installed tool, and critically its AGPL-3.0 license creates real legal exposure for a commercial SaaS backend unless we purchase an enterprise license. Not recommended given lower-friction alternatives exist.
